steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our optimization paper showing that stochastic heavy ball with step-decay learning rate schedules gets accelerated convergence on quadratic objectives under anisotropic gradient noise in large-batch settings. End with a list of our contributions.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Optimization techniques that can train large foundation models efficiently are quickly becoming more important. Mathematically, most of these optimization problems can be written as minimizing a finite sum

where numerical methods are usually used to find the minimum of this form. Of all these methods, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants are among the most widely used algorithms.

For example, heavy-ball (HB) methods, which are often called heavy-ball momentum, are one of these popular variants. In practice it was extremely helpful for speeding up the training of convolutional neural networks. In theory, it has been shown to give optimal acceleration for gradient descent (GD) on quadratic objectives.

But for SGD in theory, things are very different. Even though it is hugely successful in practice, most theoretical results on stochastic heavy ball (SHB) were negative, and showed that the convergence rates of heavy-ball methods are not better than vanilla SGD. These gaps between GD and SGD, and between practice and theory, are quite intriguing, and they make one ask: can stochastic heavy ball give \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\kappa}) accelerated convergence when the noise is small, for example in large-batch settings?

To answer this, the first step is to find what is missing in those negative results. One key observation is that all the negative results assumed constant learning rates, but in practice decaying learning rates are usually used. These decaying learning rates, often called learning rate schedules, were shown to be critical for improving the performance of a trained model in real-world tasks. Also, if we only look at the vanilla SGD algorithm, the theoretical properties of most schedules have already been well studied. Briefly, learning rate schedules can be seen as a variance reduction technique, which helps reduce the instability and deviation caused by stochastic gradient noise.

- variance reduction is key to improving SHB's rate (pointed out before) -> question: proper schedules for accelerated SHB, large batches?
- Setting
  - positive answer; quadratic objectives; simple but insights near local optimum
  - NTK: wide nets resemble NTKs, objectives approximated by quadratics
  - anisotropic SGD noise near minima (empirical), formalized in least square regression -> Assumption 3, Section 3; used by many past works

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Optimization techniques that can train large foundation models efficiently are quickly becoming more important. Mathematically, most of these optimization problems can be written as minimizing a finite sum

where numerical methods are usually used to find the minimum of this form. Of all these methods, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants are among the most widely used algorithms.

For example, heavy-ball (HB) methods, which are often called heavy-ball momentum, are one of these popular variants. In practice it was extremely helpful for speeding up the training of convolutional neural networks. In theory, it has been shown to give optimal acceleration for gradient descent (GD) on quadratic objectives.

But for SGD in theory, things are very different. Even though it is hugely successful in practice, most theoretical results on stochastic heavy ball (SHB) were negative, and showed that the convergence rates of heavy-ball methods are not better than vanilla SGD. These gaps between GD and SGD, and between practice and theory, are quite intriguing, and they make one ask: can stochastic heavy ball give \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\kappa}) accelerated convergence when the noise is small, for example in large-batch settings?

To answer this, the first step is to find what is missing in those negative results. One key observation is that all the negative results assumed constant learning rates, but in practice decaying learning rates are usually used. These decaying learning rates, often called learning rate schedules, were shown to be critical for improving the performance of a trained model in real-world tasks. Also, if we only look at the vanilla SGD algorithm, the theoretical properties of most schedules have already been well studied. Briefly, learning rate schedules can be seen as a variance reduction technique, which helps reduce the instability and deviation caused by stochastic gradient noise.

Prior work has pointed out that variance reduction is the key to improving the convergence rate of stochastic heavy ball, so it is natural to ask: are there proper learning rate schedules that help us get accelerated convergence for SHB in large-batch settings?

Our paper answers this question positively. As a first step, we restrict ourselves to quadratic objectives. These problem instances are seen as one of the simplest settings in optimization, but they give important insights for understanding how a model behaves when the parameter is close to a local optimum. Also, past literature on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) suggests that the gradient dynamics of sufficiently wide neural networks resemble NTKs, and their objectives can be approximated by quadratic objectives for specific loss functions.

Motivated by the anisotropic behavior of SGD noise observed empirically near minima of modern neural networks and the theoretical formalization of this noise property in least square regression, we do our analysis under the assumption of anisotropic gradient noise, which is formally defined later as Assumption 3 in Section 3. The very same condition has already been used or suggested by many past works.

## 1.1 Our Contributions

- 1. We introduce new theoretical techniques to analyze stochastic heavy ball with multistage schedules, and give several key properties of the 2\times 2 update matrix \mathbf{T}_{i} involved. In particular, we show that \left\|\mathbf{T}_{T-1}\mathbf{T}_{T-2}...\mathbf{T}_{0}\right\| can be upper bounded by \left\|\mathbf{T}_{T-1}^{T}\right\| under certain conditions. This lets SHB with changing learning rates have similar theoretical properties as vanilla SGD: for each eigenvalue, SHB first decreases the loss exponentially with large learning rates, and then keeps the reduced loss with small learning rates.

- 2. As a direct result of this technique, we give a non-asymptotic last iterate convergence rate for stochastic heavy ball with a step decay learning rate schedule on quadratic objectives, under the standard anisotropic gradient noise assumption. As far as we know, this is the first non-asymptotic result for SHB on quadratics that clearly shows the relationship between iteration number T, condition number \kappa and convergence rate with step-decay schedules.

- 3. Our results show that stochastic heavy ball can get near-optimal accelerated convergence in large-batch settings, and still keep the near-optimal convergence rate \tilde{O}(d\sigma^{2}/T) in variance (up to log factors away from the statistical minimax rate).

Despite its huge success in practice, most theoretical results for stochastic heavy ball (SHB) were negative, showing that the convergence rates of heavy-ball methods are no better than vanilla SGD [14,15,16,17,18,19]. These gaps between GD and SGD, and between practice and theory, are rather intriguing and may make one wonder: Can stochastic heavy ball provide \tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{\kappa}) accelerated convergence when the noise is small, such as under large-batch settings?

To answer this question, the first step is to find the missing pieces in those negative results. One key observation is that all of them assumed constant learning rates, whereas in practice decaying learning rates are usually used. These decaying learning rates, often referred to as learning rate schedules, have been demonstrated to be critical for improving the performance of a trained model in real-world tasks [20,21]. Furthermore, for the vanilla SGD algorithm, the theoretical properties of most schedules have already been well inspected [22,23,24,25,26,27]. Briefly speaking, learning rate schedules can be viewed as a variance reduction technique that helps alleviate the instability and deviation caused by stochastic gradient noise.

Since [28] pointed out that variance reduction is the key to improving stochastic heavy ball’s convergence rate, it is natural to ask: Are there proper learning rate schedules that can help us achieve accelerated convergence for SHB under large-batch settings?

Our paper gives a positive answer to this question. As a first step, we restrict ourselves to quadratic objectives. Although these problem instances are considered one of the simplest settings in optimization, they provide important insights for understanding a model’s behavior when the parameter is close to a local optimum. Furthermore, past literature on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) [29,30] suggests that the gradient dynamics of sufficiently wide neural networks resemble NTKs, and that their objectives can be approximated by quadratic objectives given specific loss functions.

Motivated by the empirical anisotropic behavior of SGD noise near minima of modern neural networks [31,32,33] and the theoretical formalization of this noise property in least square regression [34,18,26], we conduct our analysis under the assumption of anisotropic gradient noise, formally defined later as Assumption 3 in Section 3. This allows SHB with changing learning rates to exhibit theoretical properties similar to vanilla SGD: for each eigenvalue, SHB first decreases the loss exponentially with large learning rates, then retains the reduced loss with small learning rates.

As a direct result of this technical innovation, we present a non-asymptotic last iterate convergence rate for stochastic heavy ball with a step decay learning rate schedule on quadratic objectives, under the standard anisotropic gradient noise assumption. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-asymptotic result for SHB on quadratics that clearly expresses the relationship among iteration number T, condition number \kappa and convergence rate with step-decay schedules.

- 3. Our results show that stochastic heavy ball can achieve near-optimal accelerated convergence under large-batch settings, while still retaining the near-optimal convergence rate \tilde{O}(d\sigma^{2}/T) in variance (up to log factors away from the statistical minimax rate).
